title: Stop measuring tomorrow’s universities with yesterday’s metrics
summary: Donna Whitehead makes the case that successful universities in the next decade will be those who were most willing to adapt and transform
full_text:
I wasn’t supposed to go to university. Nobody in my family had done so before.

It wasn’t a path that felt designed for people like me. It was something other people’s children did.

But I did go, eventually – close to home and with no small amount of uncertainty. And it changed the course of my life.

I start there because, amid all the debate about the future of higher education, I’m increasingly struck by how rarely we discuss what universities are actually for.

Instead, much of the public conversation – particularly in the popular press – has become dominated by a different set of questions. Which universities are running deficits? Which institutions are cutting staff or recruiting fewer students? Which balance sheets appear stronger or weaker than they did twelve months ago?

These are legitimate questions. Financial sustainability matters. Universities cannot fulfil their missions if they are not financially viable.

But there is a growing risk that we confuse measures of current financial performance with measures of future institutional health.

Under pressure

The higher education sector is operating in conditions that would have been difficult to imagine even a decade ago.

Inflationary pressures, changing demographics, fluctuating demand, political uncertainty, rapidly evolving technologies and shifting employer expectations are reshaping the environment in which universities operate.

Yet many of the measures we use to assess institutional success still reflect assumptions from a different era: an era of predictable growth, expanding student numbers, and relative policy stability.

The challenge facing universities today is not recreating the conditions of 2016. It is building institutions capable of thriving in 2036.

Too often, success in our sector is framed around preservation: how do we protect existing models, maintain established structure, and navigate immediate pressures? But the bigger challenge is understanding what kind of universities tomorrow’s students, employers, and communities will need.

I believe the universities that will flourish over the next decade will be those most willing to reimagine how they teach, support their students and staff, conduct research, engage with their communities and create opportunity. They will understand that long-term success depends not on clinging to old certainties, but on building institutions that remain relevant, distinctive, and valuable in a rapidly changing world.

In that context, an institution’s willingness to reshape itself may be every bit as important as its latest financial return.

This is where I think the sector faces a profound leadership challenge.

It’s time to adapt

For understandable reasons, periods of pressure often encourage caution.

Universities reduce expenditure, postpone decisions and search for efficiencies in the hope that conditions will improve.

Sometimes those actions are necessary, but there is a danger when incremental cost-saving becomes a substitute for strategic choice.

The question cannot simply be how to preserve existing models for as long as possible. It must be whether those models remain fit for purpose.

That will be an uncomfortable conversation for many institutions. It requires university leaders and governing bodies to confront difficult questions about academic portfolios, operating models, partnerships, estates and organisational structures.

But avoiding those questions does not make them disappear.

Indeed, one of the biggest mistakes we can make is to assume that transformation is evidence of weakness. An admission of failure, even.

Too often, organisational change is interpreted as a sign that something has gone wrong. Yet in many cases the opposite may be true. Institutions that recognise shifts in their operating environment and act decisively in response may be demonstrating precisely the qualities that will define future success.

I am convinced that the strongest universities of the next decade will not be those that experienced the least disruption during this period. They will be those that were most willing to adapt and transform.

Building for the world of tomorrow

At Brighton, we have chosen to respond to these challenges through a programme of transformation designed to ensure long-term sustainability, academic distinctiveness, and radical relevance to the students and communities we serve.

We are doing what is right for our university and our place – but the principle extends far beyond any single institution.

Across the sector, leaders are grappling with the same fundamental question: how do we create universities that remain sustainable, relevant, and impactful in a very different world?

That question becomes even more urgent when we consider the students who will graduate into the economy of the 2030s.

Artificial intelligence is already reshaping how work is performed across multiple sectors. Employers are demanding different skills. Career paths are becoming even less linear and even more fluid. The knowledge, capabilities, and personal resilience students need are evolving rapidly.

In that environment, institutional success cannot be judged solely by reference to historic metrics. We should also be asking whether universities are preparing for a future that is arriving faster than many of us expected.

Are they building meaningful partnerships with employers? Are they contributing to the economic and civic life of their regions? Are they adapting their curricula and learning environments to reflect emerging realities? Are they creating opportunities for students from backgrounds traditionally underrepresented in higher education?

And are they ensuring those students are able to thrive and succeed in a way that many groups currently are not.

These are the measures that may ultimately tell us more about the long-term health of an institution than a single year’s accounts.

My own experience reminds me why that matters.

The value of the university I attended was not that it was financially solvent. It was that it created possibilities that would otherwise have remained closed to me.

And that remains the fundamental purpose of higher education.

The universities that succeed in 2036 will be the ones that were prepared to make difficult choices, embrace transformation, and redefine their role in response to a rapidly changing world.

So, rather than asking which institutions are experiencing disruption, we should be asking which institutions are using disruption to become more relevant than ever before.

The sector should not be afraid to make that case. If universities are redesigning themselves around the needs of future students, employers and communities, then we must be equally ambitious in how we explain success.

Public debate cannot remain focused solely on financial symptoms while overlooking the long-term value institutions create.

Our task now is not simply to navigate change, but to demonstrate where that change is leading.

Because the real measure of a university’s health is not what appears in last year’s accounts. It is the value it creates for the next generation.

title: Reform’s moves in local government can serve as a guide to the party’s approach to HE
summary: Through analysing what Reform UK politicians have been saying across the country, Alex Waddington and Yakub Qureshi offer advice to universities seeking to engage
full_text:
Andy Burnham entered Number 10 last week with a promise to “make politics work better.”

The new Prime Minister has a clear view of the electoral threat posed by Reform UK, as do the Labour MPs who facilitated the speedy replacement of Keir Starmer. Up until recently Nigel Farage’s party appeared to have unshakeable momentum, topping the last 300-plus national opinion polls.

Farage now faces scrutiny into the generous personal contributions and other support he has received as well as an ungainly by-election battle which, in the absence of serious competition, has taken on farcical undertones.

Yet it would be ill-advised to write off Reform as a significant political force, and to underestimate either the public’s ability to overlook its leader’s real or perceived transgressions or their growing appetite for radical new policies.

Higher education reform

Wonkhe readers will be familiar with the broad thrust of Reform’s HE policies set out in their 2024 manifesto, which included pledges to restrict undergraduate numbers and bar international student dependants.

But those in higher education – and many other sectors – face significant unknowns in dealing with a party with little in the way of historic policy or traditional base. Off-the-cuff remarks and broad rhetoric has been offered in place of explicit plans. Formal announcements contain varying degrees of detail (and are rarely collated on the party’s website).

Over the last few months, we’ve been researching the underlying messages within Reform’s communications to help organisations sensibly plan ahead. We’ve built a corpus of data from Reform’s official policies, social media feeds, and outputs from its senior officials and politicians. We’ve used text mining and natural language processing techniques to draw insights, while also interviewing more than 20 journalists who have had regular contact with Reform politicians and officials.

With the party in outright control of 24 English local authorities, there is much to be learned by how Reform has conducted its business at a council level. Witness the way the Local Government Association was dismissed by the new leader of Newcastle-Under-Lyme council as a “cosy, self-serving establishment funded by hardworking taxpayers who see absolutely nothing in return” – he went on to proclaim the relatively small saving of £17,000 a year.

Feedback from our training sessions has indicated there are a great many people who are nervous about both Reform’s policies and political style. One member of university staff who attended a recent briefing talked to us about the challenge of “constant churn” within the party leadership locally, saying:

We have got ‘in the door’ by making our focus as hyper-local as theirs. We don’t focus on national level issues. We keep our focus solely on our city. We’ve picked things we know they care about, such as defence and apprenticeships. And we’ve studiously avoided ‘culture wars’ issues such as international students, net zero, or gendered toilets.

Much of what has been said by Reform politicians hasn’t yet surfaced as formal policy – but the party’s rhetoric clearly favours some courses and disciplines over others. In an interview in June 2024, Nigel Farage told ITV that he “wouldn’t charge anyone tuition fees at university if they were studying science, technology, engineering, medicine or maths.”

Their rhetoric has demonstrated a preference for apprenticeships, degree apprenticeships, or HE courses focused on the professions or applied sciences. Our analysis of Derbyshire County Council’s communications output, looking before and after Reform took charge in May 2025, showed a notable increase in the use of the phrase “advanced manufacturing” – a nod to the presence of employers like Bombardier and Rolls Royce in the region.

The two-year undergraduate course has also been a consistent talking point – most recently in this Times interview with Reforms’s 19-year-old council leader George Finch, who has said that the university system “has to be reformed.” As he put it:

Three years at uni. You can reduce that to two and streamline education. But, no, they like the jolly. They like to sit back and have a few drinks and party.

Research and ideology

When it comes to research, Reform has kept relatively silent on matters related to funding. References to technology and innovation in our corpus of texts was limited to specific fields such as defence, construction, cryptocurrency and blockchain.

For those universities that boast research strengths in net zero, there is also a clear presentational challenge. While the party’s leadership is openly hostile to net zero and subsidies, we’ve observed that at a local government level the approach and narrative is more nuanced. For example, in the North East of England several industries in Reform-controlled authorities are involved in wind-turbine manufacture and offshore power generation, meaning that local politicians need to tread carefully.

On energy more broadly, there do appear to be opportunities as well as threats for local relationships and partnerships. Our work so far has revealed that this is one of the few policy issues prominently talked about by Reform – with household bills and the petrol pump being key platforms.

The way for universities to talk about energy (and indeed other issues) with Reform politicians is likely to be around creating jobs, prosperity and saving money for the “hardworking taxpayer” (a phrase we see used repeatedly), rather than complex economic arguments about green levies and carbon price support tax.

On other ideological issues, many will look to the US as a powerful example of higher education being used as a proxy battleground. Institutions in England already face punitive fines as a result of the free speech complaints scheme administered by the Office for Students – and manifestos for this year’s devolved elections indicated that Reform would go even harder on free speech legislation.

Following the local elections in May 2025, we saw that an immediate priority for Reform-led councils was addressing “civic pride” and “DEI” matters, making changes to policies around flag flying, promoting singing of the national anthem, and attempting to amend diversity and inclusion policies.

How to respond

It’s clear that many Reform’s policies are still being formed. While there’s nervousness about what it might mean, there’s also ground to play for.

Through structured interviews with journalists, we have observed a number of key trends when it comes to engagement with Reform:

First, the ease of communication with politicians depended on the individual’s level of political experience. Many had little previous experience and faced a steep learning curve. Politicians who had previously held office as Conservatives were more likely to follow political norms/processes.

Next, we have seen that successful engagement often involves being ready to provide a baseline understanding of what your organisation does and how it contributes to the local area or economy. Relatedly, understanding the language, priorities and ideological position of new politicians will help your early dealings. In our analysis of outputs, the phrase “common sense” came through strongly as a core phrase – one to consider if seeking to consciously “mirror” Reform-speak as part of your engagement.

It has been noted how politicians have a “public face”, meaning that in some cases they were more likely to be fractious during PR stunts, council meetings or communications with members. In private meetings, there was evidence many were more willing to engage pragmatically.

Finally, be ready for friction, including in battles which you thought were long-won. It’s helpful to have your responses prepared if things get rough. If you can, test them out in advance.

The turquoise wave

Andy Burnham’s victory in the Makerfield by-election was a solid demonstration of how Labour can potentially defend traditional Red Wall seats against the so-called “turquoise wave”. It was a resounding win and convinced Labour MPs that the Greater Manchester mayor was best placed to lead the party and the country. But for the new Prime Minister, the main battles still lie ahead.

For all the difficulties that Reform faces, the possibility of Nigel Farage entering Number 10 or becoming the leader of the opposition must still seriously be countenanced.

More generally, the underlying trend for the UK electorates’ appetite for “disruptive” parties with radical or anti-establishment ideas remains. Higher education institutions and other sector organisations would be unwise to ignore the consistent strong polling for both Reform and the Greens, especially while it remains to be seen whether Burnham’s policies and personal brand will cut through at a national level.

title: The franchise cliff edge
summary:
What happens when higher education franchise models meet tighter regulation? This analysis examines the risks for students and providers.

The post The franchise cliff edge appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr David O’Connor, Founder at Blairgowrie HE Advisory.

There are 167,440 students in subcontracted higher education arrangements in England in 2024-25. That is a 56 per cent increase since 2021-22. Of those, 113,000 are taught by organisations that are not registered with the Office for Students (OfS). The data needed to understand what this means for institutional finances, student outcomes, and lender exposure is all public. The problem is that it sits in separate places, published by separate bodies for separate purposes, and is almost always read in isolation. This piece is about what happens when you read it together.

Three cliff edges

Three regulatory events will arrive over the next two years. None of the institutions most exposed has publicly stated what it will do.

The first is already in force. Condition E10 came into effect on 31 March 2026. It compels universities to terminate arrangements where minimum standards are not met, and requires disclosure of fee-retention arrangements in future accounts.

The second is the mandatory registration deadline. Providers teaching more than 500 students must register with the OfS by 30 June 2026. Those that do not are de-designated from 2028-29. For universities that have built their financial model on franchise income, that is not a compliance task, it is an existential question.

The third is enforcement. The OfS fined Leeds Trinity £115,000 in May 2025 and imposed operational restrictions. The precedent is set.

The dependency problem

The University of Suffolk subcontracted out 77 per cent of its students in 2024-25. Canterbury Christ Church University was at 74 per cent. Bath Spa University at 73 per cent. Leeds Trinity University at 69 per cent. For these institutions, franchise income is not a supplement to the operating model. It is the operating model.

The dominant partner in several of these arrangements is Global Banking School (GBS) which is also subject to an OfS investigation that opened in January 2026 regarding its partnership with Oxford Brookes University, examining compliance with conditions on course quality, management and governance. .An estimated 38,740 students are subcontracted in from five universities, with an estimated annual revenue of £300 million. The sole person of significant control is a UAE resident. GBS has no degree-awarding powers.

The Bath Spa audited accounts tell the rest of the story. Bath Spa’s going concern note states that partnership income is “highly material.” The vice-chancellor’s foreword refers to reducing reliance on private provider franchise student numbers. Both sentences are in the same document. Meanwhile, lenders including Lloyds, Barclays, Santander, and eight US private placement holders carry exposure to institutions whose revenue base depends on arrangements that the regulatory timetable is about to disrupt.

Who these students are

At GBS, 76.6 per cent of students come from the two most deprived Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) quintiles. The sector average is 37.8 per cent. Progression to graduate-level employment is 41.8 per cent, against a benchmark of 54.2 per cent. On current student numbers, that gap generates approximately 4,800 additional non-progressors annually. Student Loans Company data shows £2.0 billion in maintenance and tuition fee loans disbursed to students at six franchise-heavy institutions in 2023-24, up from £450 million five years earlier.

These are students who enrolled on the promise of a university degree. They are predominantly from low-income backgrounds. They carry real debt. And the B3 outcome data shows they are systematically less likely to progress to graduate employment than students at their awarding institution’s own campus.

What should change

Three things would make the regulatory transition less damaging.

First, the OfS should require lead providers to publish institution-level student outcome data disaggregated by delivery partner. The data exists. It is not published in a form that prospective students, governors, or lenders can use.

Second, the Student Loans Company and the OfS should be directed to cross-reference loan disbursements against delivery location. The total public loan value flowing to non-continuing students in subcontracted provision is currently unknowable. That is a gap in public accountability, not a gap in available data.

Third, the Department for Education should set a clear expectation on transition planning. Universities with dependency ratios above 50 per cent face an acute income shock if their delivery partners fail to register. Those institutions need to publish credible transition plans before 2028, not after.

The regulatory timetable is public. The audited accounts are public. The cliff edge has a date. What is missing is any sign that the institutions walking towards it have a plan for when they reach it.

title: OPINION: Walking away from education technology isn’t the answer to the latest backlash
summary:
In too many classrooms in America, the scene is the same: children staring at tablets, headphones on, silent. Some are working through reading programs. Some have already finished and found their way to something else entirely. The teacher circulates.  The education technology industry calls this personalized learning. Somewhere, a dashboard is registering all this as […]

The post OPINION: Walking away from education technology isn’t the answer to the latest backlash appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
In too many classrooms in America, the scene is the same: children staring at tablets, headphones on, silent. Some are working through reading programs. Some have already finished and found their way to something else entirely. The teacher circulates.

The education technology industry calls this personalized learning. Somewhere, a dashboard is registering all this as engagement.

Nobody in any of those classrooms would agree. I know because I’ve spent a decade navigating this industry from the inside, building some of the technology that teachers, students and soon my own sons will use.

I’ve come to a conclusion that may surprise you: Much of the backlash against ed tech is completely justified. But it misses the broader point.

Parents are right to question whether the screens in their children’s classrooms are making them better learners. Politicians are right to demand that the industry prove it. And the nation’s largest teacher union is right to call for caution regarding screen time and student-facing AI in elementary schools.

Related: A lot goes on in classrooms from kindergarten to high school. Keep up with our free weekly newsletter on K-12 education.

These are not fringe positions. They are honest reckonings with what educators and parents have been asking the industry to confront for years. Growing alarms about the impact of screens on children’s mental health, attention spans and academic outcomes have turned a quiet concern into a political movement.

But when the responses are blanket bans and broad restrictions that make no distinction between distraction and instruction, we’re not solving a problem — we’re avoiding it.

Walking away from technology entirely isn’t protection. It’s abdication. The students in those classrooms today are inheriting a world that runs digitally and requires digital fluency.

A middle schooler who can’t evaluate an online source or the ethics of a new kind of technology isn’t a student we’ve protected. She’s a student we’ve left behind.

The answer to bad ed tech isn’t no ed tech. It’s higher standards, better tools and a philosophy that keeps teachers at the center.

That philosophy draws a clear line. Teachers should have wide access to tools that extend their reach, reduce their load and give them a real-time picture of where each student is so they can adapt instruction accordingly. But anything a student interacts with directly must clear a higher bar: It has to make the subject matter come alive in ways that simply cannot happen in print or via hands-on learning.

As a chief product officer, I make evidence-based decisions about what belongs in print, what belongs in hands-on learning and what belongs in digital form. When technology does not add real value, we choose print. But sometimes print cannot do the job.

Digital tools can help students visualize and interact with math as it appears in the world, receive immediate feedback that deepens understanding and run a science simulation that a static page simply cannot replicate.

High-quality student-facing technology should advance learning in ways that other formats cannot, strengthen rigorous classroom communities and give students authentic choices that build self-determination. From pre-K through second grade, that standard must be even higher because foundational skills are built through human interaction, not screen time.

Done right, the result sounds nothing like the opening sentences of this piece — it’s louder, messier and more alive. With purposeful technology, a teacher can see in real time that 20 of her 30 students solved a problem one way, and 10 solved it differently. She can then ask each group to explain their thinking to the other, producing something better than anything a static lesson plan can offer.

That kind of immediate feedback isn’t just good teaching. Research shows that students who receive immediate digital feedback on their work can learn significantly more than those using traditional methods.

AI is no different from other technology needing to earn its place — and no exception. The debate treats it as either a silver bullet or an existential threat. Both are wrong, yet the evidence on current AI use clearly cuts in one direction: High schoolers who studied with a general-purpose AI chatbot scored 17 percent worse on their exams.

A tool that does the thinking for students isn’t a tutor. It’s a shortcut.

Related: Teachers save time with AI. Their students may pay the price

That’s why, until we know more, I’m focused on using AI not so much with students but to help teachers with their immensely challenging jobs: supporting teachers in processing the large amount of work a class of 25 to 35 students produces; surfacing patterns before they become permanent gaps; and handling the administrative weight that pulls teachers away from teaching.

Take a math lesson in which 35 students each submit a different solution. AI can read every response, identify answers that would drive a productive math discussion and hand the teacher the information to lead a constructive conversation with students in seconds.

AI handles the analysis. The teacher handles the room. The students get a lesson built around what they actually need.

To the legislators drafting anti-tech bills and the parents and caregivers pushing for change: You are right to push. But push toward a better standard — not how many minutes students spend on screens, but whether the tools on those screens are evidence-based, whether they serve teachers or replace them and whether student data is treated as a trust rather than an asset.

Those questions cut closer to the problem than any time limit ever could.

There are signs the debate is turning. More policymakers are starting to ask about quality, not just quantity. The students caught in this debate deserve better than a narrow conversation about screens. They deserve a more honest one about which tools deepen learning and which distract from it.

Alexandra Walsh is the chief product officer at Amplify, one of the country’s largest K-12 curriculum and assessment companies. She leads the strategic vision for the company’s comprehensive math, literacy and science product suites.

Contact the opinion editor at opinion@hechingerreport.org.

This story about ed tech was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for Hechinger’s weekly newsletter.

title: New Options Emerge for Disenrolled Howard Students
summary:
New Options Emerge for Disenrolled Howard Students
Joshua.Bay Mon, 07/27/2026 - 04:58 PM

SUNY, CUNY and U of the District of Columbia are offering support and enrollment opportunities to those affected by Howard’s decision to unenroll 502 incoming students.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
The fallout from Howard University’s decision to unenroll 502 incoming students is spreading beyond the institution, with New York officials and another college moving to offer displaced students opportunities to enroll before the fall semester begins.

Howard announced last week that it had unenrolled 502 incoming students after determining they had not met payment, payment plan or financial aid requirements by university deadlines—a decision that sparked criticism from students and families who said they believed their aid was still being processed.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul announced Monday that the state will help students affected by Howard’s decision, offering guaranteed admission to participating State University of New York and City University of New York campuses for eligible New York residents.

Under the plan, SUNY and CUNY campuses with available space in their incoming classes will enroll affected students, ensuring the initiative does not reduce admission opportunities for other New York students, according to a news release from Hochul’s office. Eligible New York residents affected by Howard’s decision will be guaranteed admission to a SUNY or CUNY campus, while students from outside the state will receive expedited late admissions review at campuses with available capacity.

The SUNY campuses taking in disenrolled Howard students include Albany, Binghamton, Buffalo, Buffalo State, New Paltz, Oneonta and Stony Brook, with additional campuses reviewing available capacity. Participating CUNY colleges will be announced following consultation with campus leadership.

Students who enroll at a SUNY or CUNY institution will also receive an $800 credit to help offset the nonrefundable enrollment deposit they previously paid to Howard, the release said.

“Hundreds of students, including New Yorkers, are scrambling and scared since they’ve been disenrolled from their intended college just a few weeks before classes are set to begin,” Hochul said in the statement. “New York is home to the nation’s finest systems of public higher education, and we are ready to welcome these talented students with the opportunity they deserve. To every student who is worried that their educational future has been disrupted: New York is ready to support and empower you.”

SUNY Chancellor John B. King Jr. said in a statement, “There is a place at SUNY for every New Yorker, and we want to empower all students with access to the affordable, excellent public higher education they deserve.”

CUNY Chancellor Félix V. Matos Rodríguez said the system’s mission is to expand access to higher education and that “our doors are open” to students facing uncertainty after Howard’s decision.

It is unclear how many of the students affected by Howard’s decision are New York residents. However, enrollment data from last year shows that New York was among the top states sending students to Howard, ranking second behind Maryland.

In Washington, D.C., another institution has also stepped forward: The University of the District of Columbia, an HBCU not far from Howard, is extending its enrollment deadline to Aug. 7 for students affected by Howard’s decision, according to WUSA9.

Howard has also begun reversing some of the disenrollments. According to WJLA News 7, 46 students have been reinstated, and the university continues reviewing additional student appeals.

In a Sunday interview with CNN, Howard Interim President Wayne Frederick said it is not unusual for colleges and universities to remove students from enrollment rolls after missed deadlines. However, he noted that Howard had not previously enforced its deadlines as strictly as it did this year.

Howard did not respond by Inside Higher Ed’s deadline to a request for comment on the responses from SUNY, CUNY and the University of the District of Columbia, as well as Howard’s ongoing review of student appeals.

title: Dueling Mandates
summary:
Dueling Mandates
Sara Brady Mon, 07/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

Serve the community vs. run the college like a business.

Byline(s)
Matt Reed
full_text:
We lose a pile of money on our nursing program. Should we close it?

My personal answer is “of course not.” It’s crucial to our service area, it provides great jobs for students and with an aging population, the need for nurses is likely to continue to grow.

But if we were to run the college like a business, the answer would be to close the program. It’s a persistent money loser, and that isn’t likely to change anytime soon.

We effectively have two mandates, and they are increasingly in conflict with each other.

The first is to serve the community. That means providing opportunities for job preparation and/or transfer to higher degrees, developing the skills of civic discourse, providing cultural programming, and, most of all, offering second chances to people who need them.

The second is to “run it like a business.” That means keeping costs down, trimming low-enrolled or money-losing programs and generally minimizing what legislators have to provide.

The conflict is clear in an area like nursing. We can provide what the community needs, or we can close money-losing programs. But we can’t do both fully. The only way to make that math work would be to raise tuition to levels that would defeat the access side of the mission, and that would rightly generate toxic political pushback.

If the issue were confined to nursing, it would be straightforward enough. But consistently, the programs employers demand tend to be money losers for us. In a sense, that’s why employers demand them—training in specialized fields is expensive, and they’d rather socialize the costs than pay for them themselves. Given employee mobility, there’s an argument for that. But to then turn around and admonish the institution that picks up the expensive programs for not running even leaner than it already does is a bit much.

Grants help, of course. Perkins has done a lot of heavy lifting over the years, and various other grants and scholarships have made programs possible. But those are subject to the whims of funders and/or legislators, and as we’ve learned over the past few years, those can change quickly and arbitrarily. As welcome as grants and donations are, they aren’t as reliable as income over expenses derived from operations.

As state and local funding have lagged, the tension between the two imperatives get harder to ignore every year.

That tension has really come to a head with dual enrollment. Colleges acting like businesses are crowding into high schools. In states without meaningful ground rules, that quickly becomes a race to the bottom in terms of both funding and academic standards. High schools openly play colleges off against each other, with “winning” coming down to who is the most academically and financially lenient.

Yes, financial responsibility is important. As stewards of public funds, there’s a responsibility to use resources wisely. But at a certain point, the mission requires what the mission requires. The expensive equipment, small class sizes and faculty with specialized knowledge in high-demand fields cost money.

title: Can Outcomes-Based Financing Help Solve the Loan Crisis?
summary:
Can Outcomes-Based Financing Help Solve the Loan Crisis?
jessica.blake@… Mon, 07/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

In an interview with Inside Higher Ed, Ethan Pollack, a senior director at Jobs for the Future, discusses how these loans work and why they might help address today’s challenges.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
Starting this academic year, graduate students will face new federal borrowing limits, driving some to private lenders and leaving others without a way to finance their education. But a group of bipartisan lawmakers and policy experts believes they have a solution to this funding gap: outcomes-based financing.

Now, they’re looking to pass a bill that would make it possible.

Introduced last month by a group of bipartisan, bicameral lawmakers, the Outcomes-Based Financing for Students Act is designed to create a framework that helps a lender tie students’ loan access to their earnings after graduation rather than to their credit history. It includes safeguards such as capping payments at no more than 20 percent of a student’s income, providing additional protections for lower-income students who earn less than 350 percent of the federal poverty level and requiring clear, standardized disclosures about what borrowers are getting themselves into before they sign on the dotted line, among other things.

The lawmakers say they hope to “expand access to innovative financing options for students pursuing postsecondary education and workforce training.”

To develop the bill, the lawmakers worked with policy experts from Jobs For the Future, a nonprofit group focused on workforce and economic development. Inside Higher Ed spoke with Ethan Pollack, a senior director at JFF, to break down how these loans work, why they matter now and how they might address today’s challenges while preparing students and colleges across the country for the years ahead.

The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: Let’s start with the basics: What exactly is outcomes-based financing?

A: Outcomes-based financing is any type where how much the students repay is in part based off of their earnings. This can be done in a couple ways.

The easiest way is what you might call an outcomes-based loan, which is like a normal loan, except the repayments have some type of income contingency. So a good example of that would be an earnings threshold. In any given month, if the student is earning below a certain threshold that’s set in the contract, then they would make no payments in that month. You can also have a time-based obligation, where after a period of time, no matter how much the student has repaid, at the end of that period of time, their obligation to pay expires.

You can also design it as an income-share agreement as well [which offers students up-front financial support in exchange for a portion of their future earnings for a set number of years]. There’s some subtle differences. ISAs can potentially be a little more complicated and harder for the student to understand. Providers usually have to do a lot more work in making sure that this is something that actually students understand they’re signing up for.

In both cases, you are trying to tailor how much the students pay to how much they’re earning over a period of time, and that in theory—if these are designed well, which is a big if—can make education over all more affordable.

Q: It sounds like you think this can be a better solution than traditional fixed-rate loans for some students. Why is that?

A: First off, it can be a better option. It’s not always a better option; it depends on whether it’s designed well.

So, how? I think in two ways: One, it can be more accessible to students who have thin credit files or do not have parents that can co-sign. Outcomes-based financing payments are based more on outcomes. That means the underwriting and the criteria of eligibility for these products can be designed to de-emphasize things like credit score and having a co-signer. Instead, they are now tracking what we expect your earnings to be based on the program you’re enrolled in.

The second way is that when they’re in repayment, if they have lower earnings than expected, or they suffer some type of shock—a recession, a pandemic, all of these things can happen that can lead to students not getting the earnings that they thought they might get—an outcomes-based financing tool provides flexibility for those borrowers. You can say that the outcomes-based financing bends when life bends. It is not that type of rigid repayment that could create a kind of financial albatross for that student.

Q: So, how does this legislation change what can be considered in underwriting? Because my understanding is that currently many lenders believe the outcomes-based factors you mentioned can’t be considered without violating the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, a law that prohibits creditors from discriminating against credit applicants on the basis of group characteristics like race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age.

A: I should say, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act does not prohibit providers from using outcomes-based financing, and there are lenders that already do this today. But the vast majority of lenders avoid using outcomes data in their underwriting because it subjects them to regulatory risk, which makes them nervous, even if what they’re doing is perfectly legal. So for lenders that offer outcomes-based financing, this bill creates more clarity and assurance that they can use certain outcomes metrics, like completion rates or median earnings, as part of an empirically derived methodology. They’re still subject to the Equal Credit Opportunity Act; this bill simply provides more clarity in how to comply with it. And I think there’s a really good reason for that: Right now there’s a disparate impact in education.

In particular, if you think of some really low-performing or predatory schools—who tends to be the victims of those schools? They tend to be students who come from those [Equal Credit Opportunity Act]–protected classes; just the provision of education itself oftentimes has a disparate impact.

If I’m an outcomes-based financing lender, I don’t want to be lending to students that are attending schools that have really horrible completion rates, because I don’t think that those schools are serving their students. I don’t want to perpetuate that bad business model. But currently there’s a perverse aspect of the Equal Credit Opportunity Act that in theory could actually force the lender to be providing financing to those students and enhance disparate impact.

What this legislation is saying is that you need to allow providers of outcomes-based financing to take into account some of the outcomes metrics to ensure that they are only financing students at schools where they are actually going to serve the students.

Q: So what’s the incentive for lenders in this system of outcomes-based loans?

A: It’s a good question. When JFF has been doing this legislation, the organizations we partner with generally are nonprofit providers with outcomes-based financing. So these are lenders that are not trying to really make a profit; they’re just trying to be sustainable. Sometimes the goal is not even to be sustainable, but rather to simply recycle some portion of the revenue back.

Social Finance is a really good example of this. They offer zero-interest outcomes-based loans for a certain segment of their programs, so they’re not making a profit on that. They’re not even recouping, but nonetheless it can be a better philanthropic approach. Rather than simply providing the service for free [like a scholarship], they’re able to make sure that some recipients of those services pay back and then they can then recycle that money and expand access to even more students than otherwise would be eligible.

For more for-profit options or ones trying to provide some kind of return on capital, I think it’s actually really useful to look at some of the research that came out of Purdue University. Purdue had an income-share agreement program from 2017 to 2022, and they recently did research showing that about two-thirds of the students in their program paid less than they otherwise would have under a comparable fixed-payment loan.

Now that means that one-third of the students ended up paying a little more than they would have under that comparable fixed-payment loan—and that kind of answers your question. Under this type of approach, some students pay more and some students pay less. Which ones pay more and which ones pay less is entirely dependent on their earnings.

It’s less about how they profit from it. You’re just redistributing the repayment away from low-earning students and toward more of the high-earning students.

Q: What are some obstacles to scaling up outcomes-based options for students?

A: Right now there are a lot of regulatory guardrails, which were designed to protect students, that are actually standing in the way of students having these more affordable options.

Imagine that you’re a car manufacturer, and yet you’re subject to all of the rules and regulations for home building. So you’re building a car, but the car has to have an earthquake-resistant foundation. That would be really weird. But it would also not protect consumers, because that’s not a form of consumer protection that makes sense for cars. In fact, they’d be less protected, because it wouldn’t say anything about seat belts, airbags or crumple zones.

The point here is that in that circumstance, the consumer protections are poorly designed for the product, and so therefore you end up with the worst of all outcomes. That’s where we are at with outcomes-based financing. In addition, we recognize that there is risk to some of these as well. It’s possible for a provider to design one that is predatory, and so we also want to make sure that the consumers are protected.

There are a number of changes that can be made to accomplish that. One is adjusting underwriting regulations, as discussed previously. Another is around disclosures.

The federal Truth in Lending Act was really built for fixed-payment loans and just is not well suited for outcomes-based financing. An example is that the act requires disclosure of the loan’s annual percentage rate, or the APR. But the APR of an outcomes-based financing tool can vary widely from student to student, because how much they pay back actually depends on what their future incomes are going to be. So, what we’ve proposed in this bill is amending the Truth in Lending Act to ensure that the outcomes-based loans have more customized or unique disclosure guidelines. They still need to provide standardized and conspicuous disclosures, but they need to do so on outcomes-based financing–specific terms.

Q: Would this legislation also allow traditional lenders to consider some of those forward-looking characteristics? For example, could they take into account the cohort default rate of an institution rather than look at the financial history of an individual and their family?

A: It would not, and that’s because the legislation is specifically designed to only apply to outcomes-based financing, and there’s a reason for that. We didn’t want to be changing the rules of the road for all loans.

Now, what this legislation would do is create space for those students to be served with outcomes-based financing products, which will shift risk away from the student. As to whether it could lead to some other type of legislation for fixed-rate loans, I’m not sure. Maybe if this is successful it could, or maybe we just decide that we’re really happy with them being served by these really student-friendly outcomes-based financing products, and we can just leave it at that.

title: 'I was freaking out,' says Howard student among 500 unenrolled over tuition payment
summary: Several frustrated families said they traveled hours to Washington, D.C., seeking accountability from the school.
full_text:
Howard University has reinstated dozens of the more than 500 incoming first-year students it unenrolled last week over missed tuition and financial-aid deadlines, leaving hundreds still without a place in the class weeks before the fall semester begins.

While some are breathing a sigh of relief, many prospective students have been left in limbo and in a state of confusion -- some traveling to Washington, D.C. from all across the country to attempt to resolve the situation in person.

Last week, the university said 502 students missed a critical tuition payment deadline that would have otherwise secured their registration for the Fall 2026 semester, which starts on August 17.

The school claims that students received a wide range of tuition and financial aid deadline notifications beginning in March, with additional notifications every month, including in July ahead of the school's July 10 deadline that reminded incoming freshmen to submit their tuition payments.

But some incoming students claim they never received a notification at all. Others told ABC News that the only notification they received regarding the tuition payment deadline came the day it was due, sending people like Nikiyah Clark, a 17-year-old incoming freshman, scrambling to try and find the funds last minute -- causing her to miss the deadline.

The next notice Clark said she received was one unenrolling her from the school. Clark told ABC News she took a Greyhound bus at 2:30 a.m. Monday in an attempt to regain her spot at the school.

“I was freaking out,” Clark said when she received a notice from the school that stated that she had been unenrolled. “I was so scared because Howard University is my dream school, like, my grandma went there,” she said.

“On July 22, on a Wednesday, I got this email to my Howard email, and basically it says, you have declined your offer to attend Howard University,” Clark explained, adding, “However, I never did that, so I was kind of confused.”

“Then I got another email around 3:00 p.m., like, a couple hours later, basically saying you missed the July 10 payment and -- because of that -- because you missed the July 10 payment, you will not be able to attend our university. All decisions are final,” Clark told ABC News.

In a statement, Howard’s office of communications is standing by the school's decision, stressing that its enforcement actions are to “ensure the University can appropriately allocate resources to support all enrolled students.”

Howard explained that students who didn’t complete their “established payment, payment arrangement, or scholarship and other financial aid reporting deadlines” have been denied enrollment.

ABC News was not immediately able to determine why accounts from the university and some of its incoming freshmen differed regarding the communications from the school reminding incoming students about their payment deadline.

A spokesperson for Howard declined to provide ABC News with the documentation of the notifications it claims to have sent to incoming students.

Howard did not directly address the communications discrepancies but said it’s “reviewing information related to enrollment status, anticipated scholarship funding, and other financial aid, where appropriate.”

It is expected to provide updates on the reenrollment numbers later this week, according to the spokesperson.

But Erin Lynch, the president of Quality Education for Minorities (QEM) Network, a non-profit education organization, explained that what happened at Howard is typical at most higher education institutions.

“Universities do drop deadline dates,” Lynch told ABC News. “They set drop deadline dates for students because you know they need to have secured payments in place before they can actually have students show up on campus, so what happened is standard across colleges and universities across the country,” she said.

The Howard spokesperson said in previous years it has been standard practice to unenroll a small number of incoming freshmen who have missed tuition deadlines. With newly appointed enrollment officials in the admissions office, the school is now cracking down even harder on missed payments, according to the spokesperson.

Meanwhile, several frustrated families who said they traveled hours to D.C. seeking accountability from the school were still waiting in the queue at the school's administration building as of Monday evening.

Rasha Jackson, whose cousin is an incoming first-year student from California, said she waited more than six hours on behalf of the family before she was seen by a school representative.

With school starting for all students in just three weeks, Jackson said her cousin still hasn't been reinstated.

“It's just like no one [in administration] cares,” Jackson told ABC News. “That's the disappointing part about it because, you know, I advocate strongly for HBCUs. I always encourage students, ‘Hey, apply to that HBCU,’ let's go where we're gonna be accepted and appreciated and not tolerated,” she said.

“This is a big slap in our face,” she added.

title: The international student recruitment industry needs a reset
summary:
As student expectations shift and competition intensifies, institutions can no longer measure success by enrolment figures alone. Lasting success depends on trust, partnerships and supporting students long after they submit an application, says Hitanshu Bhardwaj.

The post The international student recruitment industry needs a reset appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Measuring the success of international student recruitment used to be all about how many students enrolled. But times have changed, and now it’s not just about the numbers. Sure, having more students enroll is still important, but it’s no longer the only way to define success in the global education sector. These days, there’s more to it than just counting how many students show up on campus each semester.

International student recruitment is not about selling products and it should not be treated like one. The students are making life-changing decisions that would impact their professional, financial and personal future.

Earlier with lack of information available students were dependent on recruitment consultants to give them more information on Universities, programs and other factors but now students around the world have more knowledge about these information than ever before. They compare destinations on different parameters to which they used to do earlier. The change in student thinking has also changed the student recruitment models around the world.

This shift demands a different approach from universities and recruitment partners alike.

In today’s recruitment world the recruitment strategy begins long before an application is submitted. The first step is building the institution brand in the local market,understanding cultural expectations, and creating genuine relationships with schools, counselors, education partners, and families. Trust cannot be built during an admissions cycle—it is earned over years of consistent engagement.

This shift demands a different approach from universities and recruitment partners alike

Every market is different and it is equally important to understand. A student in India would differ in terms of what factors influence them to choose an institution or a country to study than a student from Uzbekistan, Nepal, Philippines or UAE. So for every region the institution needs recruitment partners who not only deliver applications but can also provide market intelligence, identify emerging trends and position the institution according to the needs of the students from the region. In today’s recruitment environment Institutions need recruitment partners who are strategic advisors rather than sales channels.

As the world of international education gets tougher, schools need to think differently about what it means to be successful. It’s not just about filling up classrooms with students. A truly successful intake is one where students are ready to learn, get the support they need, stay on track, and eventually become graduates who make their school proud.

The future belongs to universities that are willing to listen more, collaborate more closely, and invest in relationships rather than transactions. International education has always been about creating opportunities across borders. Recruitment is simply the first chapter of that journey—not the destination itself.

If we can shift our focus from recruitment to student success, from transactions to partnerships, and from short-term targets to long-term impact, we will build a stronger, more sustainable future for international education.

We should be focusing on having that exact conversation in our industry.

About the author: With over 17 years of experience in international education, Hitanshu Bhardwaj specialises in global student recruitment, transnational partnerships, and market expansion strategies. As the director of global strategy and partnerships at University Consulting, he works closely with universities and education partners to develop sustainable recruitment networks across South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, and other emerging markets.

Throughout his career, he has collaborated with institutions worldwide to strengthen international enrolments, build high-performing agent networks, and identify new growth opportunities. His expertise spans international admissions, strategic partnerships, business development, and market intelligence, with a strong focus on ethical recruitment and long-term institutional success.

A regular participant at leading global education events, including The Pie Live, NAFSA and ICEF, he is passionate about connecting institutions with quality recruitment partners and creating meaningful opportunities for students to access world-class education.

His mission is simple: to help universities expand globally through trusted partnerships, innovative recruitment strategies, and a student-first approach to international education.

title: Review: Canva for Campus Provides a Shared Platform for Visual Communication
summary:
Universities produce an enormous amount of visual content. Faculty members create lecture presentations and course materials. Marketing teams produce event promotions and recruitment campaigns. Students generate slides, videos and graphics for coursework. But keeping all of those efforts coordinated while maintaining quality and brand consistency can be difficult.
Canva for Campus is designed to simplify that process by providing a shared platform where students, faculty and staff can design, collaborate and publish visual materials without needing specialized design software.
Canva for…
full_text:
Maintaining Brand Consistency Across Campus

Large universities often operate like small cities. Each department, program and student organization produces its own communications, from event posters and social media graphics to course materials and recruitment content.

While this artistic diversity is valuable, it can also create challenges when institutions try to maintain consistent branding. Logos, color palettes and typography can vary widely across departments, which makes it harder for universities to present a unified identity.

Canva for Campus addresses this common issue with shared templates and brand management tools. Administrators can create standardized design templates that reflect official branding guidelines. These templates can then be used by faculty, staff and students as starting points for their own materials.

During my testing, the availability of prebuilt layouts made it easy to produce original content that still aligned with institutional style guidelines. For example, if a university uses a specific color scheme, that can be applied to all materials regardless of what department is producing them.

Of course, users can customize text and images as needed, but can also preserve consistent design elements such as logos, fonts and colors that represent their school or campus. And that balance between structure and flexibility is particularly useful in higher education environments, where many contributors create content but few people are trained designers.

By centralizing templates and design resources, Canva for Campus allows universities to encourage creativity while still maintaining a recognizable institutional identity. Over time, that consistency can strengthen branding across everything from classroom presentations to campuswide marketing campaigns.

title: Beyond export: rethinking transnational education partnerships
summary: The post Beyond export: rethinking transnational education partnerships appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Dr Sathees Kunjuthamby, Senior Lecturer & International Partnerships Link Tutor, University of Greenwich, shares his experience on bridging UK quality expectations with host-country realties.

The current transnational higher education landscape

Transnational higher education (TNE) is where recognised UK degree-awarding bodies deliver higher education-level awards in a country, or to students other than the awarding provider’s country of operation. TNE includes several forms of delivery such as distance, online, face-to-face and hybrid (QAA 2026). TNE plays a significant role in UK higher education. According to a recent report from QAA (2026), the 2024-25 data recorded that 184 UK providers engage in TNE provision in 233 countries and territories and the trend is not expected to decline, on the contrary, it is expected that that education exports to £40 billion per year by 2030 as stated by the UK Government’s International Education Strategy report (DfE, DBT and FCDO 2026).

The growing strategic importance of UK transnational education

As a result of this, many UK universities, both with extensive experience in TNE delivery and those newer to the TNE landscape, are investing their time and effort in identifying and developing meaningful and sustainable international partnerships and TNE provision. Countries such as Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Singapore and Egypt are emerging as the five leading host countries (QAA 2026).

Experience as an External Advisor in TNE

I’ve acted as an external advisor for UK universities and contributed to on-site advisory reviews, franchise approvals, course and institutional validation events in India, the UAE, Sri Lanka, Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Spain (remotely). These processes involve evaluating a range of academic and quality assurance documentation to assess whether the TNE partner can deliver the franchised programmes responsibly and effectively without compromising on student experience and quality of the higher education provision.

The tension: standardisation vs context

The central argument of this article is that successful TNE requires moving beyond standardised or export-driven models towards more context-sensitive, collaborative approaches that recognise both the strengths and constraints of partner institutions.

Regulatory environments

UK universities seeking to develop TNE partnerships must navigate host-country regulatory environments. For example, in Hong Kong the HKCAAVQ (Hong Kong Council for Accreditation of Academic and Vocational Qualifications) plays a key role in monitoring and ensuring that the local as well as the non-local higher education provider maintain and sustain the quality of the delivered programmes. Changes in government policy and requirements can also affect the TNE delivery and contribute to limited host-country collaboration, ultimately leading to discontinuation with the proposed programmes.

Pedagogical traditions

Pedagogical traditions vary across each country, and their traditions are strongly influenced by the local context. Sri Lanka, India and Malaysia, for example, are historically examination oriented with emphasis on strong teacher-led instruction, while Singapore promotes active learning, problem-solving and industry engagement. I have also seen significant variations in student-teacher relationships, learning expectations (self-directed learning vs guided learning), feedback expectations, academic support, classroom participation and the overall curriculum orientation (theoretical knowledge vs applied and employability focused learning).

Digital readiness

This often refers to the institutional digital infrastructure, student and staff digital literacy, learning management systems (LMS) and the reliability of internet access. Across all countries, both students and staff demonstrate a high level of digital literacy, and hold a well-established infrastructure, which indicates strong readiness to support TNE delivery and provides UK higher education institutions with confidence in the partner’s ability to deliver programmes effectively.

Institutional capacity

A benefit of these events is the opportunity to experience the institution in person, rather than through reading documentation and virtual meetings. Visits are valuable and important, as they help build trust, demonstrate mutual commitment, strengthen relationships and ensure everyone involved in the process feels valued. On site visits also offer the panel deeper levels of scrutiny because of their significant implications for investment, sustainability and reputation.

Direct engagement with academic leaders, staff and students often provide valuable context, improving the understanding of the submitted documentation. We gain more insights into the academic leadership, student support services and matters relating to social, recreational and welfare facilities. We can assess learning spaces, digital infrastructure and operational arrangements and can quickly escalate and address emerging issues in a constructive and collaborative manner. For example, institutions in Sri Lanka, Singapore, Hong Kong and Malaysia are investing in high-tech learning spaces supporting a better student experience and providing strong support for blended and online learning.

The challenge: aligning standards

The evidence I have encountered across the countries I have visited suggests that one of the most significant challenges in TNE is the tension between maintaining UK academic standards and accommodating the realities of local delivery contexts. We must acknowledge the local context, collaborate with the partners and adapt our delivery appropriately, whilst maintaining UK academic standards through the partnership.

UK universities should not enforce the UK model as a default and expect their international partners to replicate the model in its entirety (over-standardisation). While it is important for UK universities to seek assurance that academic quality, integrity and student outcomes remain comparable with other UK HE institutions, they must acknowledge that TNE partners operate in a different environment, where local realities are shaped by a different regulatory environment, educational traditions and resource environments. This may limit the scope of uniformity; however, it moves away from a ‘tick-box’ approach and prioritises and increases attention on teaching and learning, student success and support.

What have I learned?

TNE with UK HE institutions does not require replicating the UK model. Instead, sustainable partnerships are built on local relevance, joint problem-solving and mutual learning. In other words, moving away from the traditional ‘export model’ to ‘co-creation’, whilst still maintaining and reassuring UK academic standards.

title: Università pubblica: la politica del soffocamento e la resa dei rettori
summary: Non si ferma il soffocamento dell’università pubblica. E’ confermato che nel 2026 il finanziamento complessivo non registrerà alcun aumento reale. Ora è in arrivo il decreto con cui il fondo verrà ripartito tra gli atenei: non solo poche risorse, ma regole di distribuzione che condannano al declino la maggior parte delle università italiane. Lo scorso […]
full_text:
Non si ferma il soffocamento dell’università pubblica. E’ confermato che nel 2026 il finanziamento

complessivo non registrerà alcun aumento reale. Ora è in arrivo il decreto con cui il fondo verrà

ripartito tra gli atenei: non solo poche risorse, ma regole di distribuzione che condannano al declino

la maggior parte delle università italiane.

Lo scorso 26 giugno, al Tecnopolo Dama di Bologna, la ministra Anna Maria Bernini aveva

annunciato con toni trionfali (nel pieno stile autocelebrativo di questo governo) 50 milioni di euro

aggiuntivi per l’FFO, il fondo di finanziamento ordinario. Una cifra irrisoria rispetto a un fondo che

vale circa 9,4 miliardi. Ma comunque quell’aumento, nella sostanza, non c’è. Il fondo complessivo

rimane praticamente fermo in termini nominali e risulta persino ridotto se si considera che nella sua

composizione entrano partite spostate da altri capitoli, come il piano straordinario per i ricercatori

del Pnrr (circa 11 milioni di euro), che, per altro, stabilizzerà solo una minima parte degli oltre

ottomila precari con contratto in scadenza (perché sottodimensionato rispetto a quanto sarebbe

necessario, e perché sarà solo in parte utilizzato da diversi atenei per ragioni che sarebbe

interessante approfondire).

Sancito il sottofinanziamento, è in arrivo ora il decreto di riparto. La bozza è pronta e ha appena

ricevuto (il 23 luglio) parere favorevole dal Consiglio universitario, proprio mentre lo stesso Cun è

sotto attacco, per essere ridotto a spettatore passivo da un progetto di riforma già al Senato.

I numeridella bozza raccontano una spartizione impietosa: 53 atenei su 66 avranno nominalmente un

incremento dello 0%, che in realtà, considerando inflazione e spostamento di partite di bilancio,

significa un arretramento. E poteva venire fuori qualcosa di perfino peggiore, se si considera che è

solo attraverso un patto solidaristico tra atenei che la clausola di salvaguardia ha fermato le

variazioni minime allo 0% (per molti atenei altrimenti si sarebbe avuta una variazione negativa

rispetto al 2025, anche in termini nominali).

Questo è il risultato dell’imposizione, da parte del ministero, di un meccanismo di riparto fondato

su criteri dimensionali (non è un percorso iniziato da questo governo, ma questo governo persevera

sulla stessa disastrosa strada).

Due terzi dell’FFO (il rimanente è prevalentemente attribuito via quota storica) vengono distribuiti

attraverso due algoritmi. Il primo è il famigerato costo standard, basato sul numero di studenti. È il

dispositivo che spinge gli atenei a inseguire iscritti in ogni modo possibile, alimentando derive da

“laureificio” sempre più vicine al modello delle telematiche: corsi online senza adeguate

infrastrutture, abbassamento della qualità, corsi acchiappa-iscritti al posto dei saperi che non fanno

massa ma restano strategici per il paese.

Un meccanismo suicida se si guarda alla demografia: l’Istat certifica che le nascite in Italia sono

crollate di oltre un terzo dal 2010 a oggi, e questo significa che nei prossimi quindici anni la platea

potenziale di studenti si ridurrà nella stessa proporzione. Ancorare il finanziamento a un numero di

iscritti che strutturalmente si assottiglia condanna gli atenei medi e piccoli a una asfissia lenta e

programmata. La quota riferibile al costo standard, per di più, nel 2026 aumenta, passando dal 36%

al 38% dell’FFO.

Il secondo algoritmo è la cosiddetta quota premiale. Ma di premiale ha pochissimo. Per come è

calcolata, la quota premiale si rivela quasi perfettamente proporzionale alla dimensione degli organici.

Il sistema di valutazione della ricerca, infatti, oltre a essere contestato da larga parte della

comunità scientifica, incide molto meno di quanto la retorica ministeriale lasci intendere e finisce

per pesare pochissimo sull’FFO: conta chi ha più docenti, non chi fa ricerca di qualità.

Messi insieme, i due meccanismi innescano una spirale, che fa arrivare le briciole ai pochi atenei

già forti, mentre il resto del sistema arretra. La ragione è semplice da comprendere: i criteri di

riparto definiscono come distribuire una torta che non cresce (cioè l’FFO complessivo), e se alcuni

(pochissimi) atenei prendono più risorse, gli altri (molti) inevitabilmente ne prendono sempre di

meno. Anno dopo anno, il grosso del sistema universitario è quindi costretto a tagliare servizi,

offerta didattica, progettualità scientifica e reclutamento, perdendo studenti e organico, avvitandosi

in un pericoloso circolo vizioso, da cui sarà sempre più difficile uscire.

Questa non è la conseguenza di una sbadata scelta tecnica. E’ bensì il prodotto della consapevole

scelta politica di svuotare la funzione sociale dell’università pubblica come strumento di coesione,

mobilità e produzione di conoscenza. Da un lato, le telematiche continuano a beneficiare di regole

di favore nei requisiti di accreditamento: basti pensare che hanno quintuplicato (+468%) i propri

iscritti nell’ultimo decennio. Dall’altra, gli atenei pubblici vengono spinti verso una gestione sempre

più contabile e di pura sopravvivenza, che azzera la missione culturale delle università e la loro

capacità strategica.

Non sorprende, ma preoccupa, che la Conferenza dei rettori (la Crui) si divida tra chi gioca la

propria partita da una posizione di vantaggio e chi si appiattisce sulla linea della ministra, per

affinità politica o per timore. Rettori forti in casa propria, deboli di fronte al governo (con solo

alcune, pochissime, voci fuori dal coro). Un’amara delusione, perché sarebbe invece possibile

costruire un fronte comune di opposizione a una politica ormai pluriennale di strozzamento

dell’università. Da chi rappresenta la voce delle comunità universitarie, ci si aspetterebbe ben altra

visione.

Il quadro si completa con l’offensiva sulla governance: la riforma del reclutamento, già approvata al

Senato, che abolisce l’ASN e spinge ad un salto nel vuoto, tra rischi di localismo e opacità nella

gestione dei concorsi (difficile, ad oggi, prevederne le conseguenze); la riforma del Cun, che lo

relegherà a una posizione di subalternità rispetto al ministero, con la rappresentanza di ricercatori e

studenti tagliata; la (per ora arenata) riforma proposta della commissione presieduta da Ernesto

Galli della Loggia, che mirerebbe a rafforzare ulteriormente i rettori e i consigli di amministrazione

a scapito della partecipazione delle comunità universitarie.

È la parabola aperta dalla legge Gelmini, che aveva già spostato il baricentro a favore dei consigli

d’amministrazione, per arrivare, alla fine, a università governate come aziende, verticalizzate e prive

di democrazia interna, non come istituzioni culturali.

Il precipitato di tutto questo non è solo precariato, tagli e divari territoriali in crescita. È la perdita,

pezzo dopo pezzo, di uno dei luoghi in cui si costruisce conflitto, discussione, progetto: uno dei

pilastri dell’infrastruttura democratica del paese. Forse è proprio questo l’obiettivo. La storia ci ha

già mostrato dove portano le società che impoveriscono sistematicamente i propri luoghi di

conoscenza. Il problema non è soltanto la caduta. È l’atterraggio.
translated_text:
Non si ferma il soffocamento dell’università pubblica. E’ confermato che nel 2026 il finanziamento

complessivo non registrerà alcun aumento reale. Ora è in arrivo il decreto con cui il fondo verrà

ripartito tra gli atenei: non solo poche risorse, ma regole di distribuzione che condannano al declino

la maggior parte delle università italiane.

Lo scorso 26 giugno, al Tecnopolo Dama di Bologna, la ministra Anna Maria Bernini aveva

annunciato con toni trionfali (nel pieno stile autocelebrativo di questo governo) 50 milioni di euro

aggiuntivi per l’FFO, il fondo di finanziamento ordinario. Una cifra irrisoria rispetto a un fondo che

vale circa 9,4 miliardi. Ma comunque quell’aumento, nella sostanza, non c’è. Il fondo complessivo

rimane praticamente fermo in termini nominali e risulta persino ridotto se si considera che nella sua

composizione entrano partite spostate da altri capitoli, come il piano straordinario per i ricercatori

del Pnrr (circa 11 milioni di euro), che, per altro, stabilizzerà solo una minima parte degli oltre

ottomila precari con contratto in scadenza (perché sottodimensionato rispetto a quanto sarebbe

necessario, e perché sarà solo in parte utilizzato da diversi atenei per ragioni che sarebbe

interessante approfondire).

Sancito il sottofinanziamento, è in arrivo ora il decreto di riparto. La bozza è pronta e ha appena

ricevuto (il 23 luglio) parere favorevole dal Consiglio universitario, proprio mentre lo stesso Cun è

sotto attacco, per essere ridotto a spettatore passivo da un progetto di riforma già al Senato.

I numeridella bozza raccontano una spartizione impietosa: 53 atenei su 66 avranno nominalmente un

incremento dello 0%, che in realtà, considerando inflazione e spostamento di partite di bilancio,

significa un arretramento. E poteva venire fuori qualcosa di perfino peggiore, se si considera che è

solo attraverso un patto solidaristico tra atenei che la clausola di salvaguardia ha fermato le

variazioni minime allo 0% (per molti atenei altrimenti si sarebbe avuta una variazione negativa

rispetto al 2025, anche in termini nominali).

Questo è il risultato dell’imposizione, da parte del ministero, di un meccanismo di riparto fondato

su criteri dimensionali (non è un percorso iniziato da questo governo, ma questo governo persevera

sulla stessa disastrosa strada).

Due terzi dell’FFO (il rimanente è prevalentemente attribuito via quota storica) vengono distribuiti

attraverso due algoritmi. Il primo è il famigerato costo standard, basato sul numero di studenti. È il

dispositivo che spinge gli atenei a inseguire iscritti in ogni modo possibile, alimentando derive da

“laureificio” sempre più vicine al modello delle telematiche: corsi online senza adeguate

infrastrutture, abbassamento della qualità, corsi acchiappa-iscritti al posto dei saperi che non fanno

massa ma restano strategici per il paese.

Un meccanismo suicida se si guarda alla demografia: l’Istat certifica che le nascite in Italia sono

crollate di oltre un terzo dal 2010 a oggi, e questo significa che nei prossimi quindici anni la platea

potenziale di studenti si ridurrà nella stessa proporzione. Ancorare il finanziamento a un numero di

iscritti che strutturalmente si assottiglia condanna gli atenei medi e piccoli a una asfissia lenta e

programmata. La quota riferibile al costo standard, per di più, nel 2026 aumenta, passando dal 36%

al 38% dell’FFO.

Il secondo algoritmo è la cosiddetta quota premiale. Ma di premiale ha pochissimo. Per come è

calcolata, la quota premiale si rivela quasi perfettamente proporzionale alla dimensione degli organici.

Il sistema di valutazione della ricerca, infatti, oltre a essere contestato da larga parte della

comunità scientifica, incide molto meno di quanto la retorica ministeriale lasci intendere e finisce

per pesare pochissimo sull’FFO: conta chi ha più docenti, non chi fa ricerca di qualità.

Messi insieme, i due meccanismi innescano una spirale, che fa arrivare le briciole ai pochi atenei

già forti, mentre il resto del sistema arretra. La ragione è semplice da comprendere: i criteri di

riparto definiscono come distribuire una torta che non cresce (cioè l’FFO complessivo), e se alcuni

(pochissimi) atenei prendono più risorse, gli altri (molti) inevitabilmente ne prendono sempre di

meno. Anno dopo anno, il grosso del sistema universitario è quindi costretto a tagliare servizi,

offerta didattica, progettualità scientifica e reclutamento, perdendo studenti e organico, avvitandosi

in un pericoloso circolo vizioso, da cui sarà sempre più difficile uscire.

Questa non è la conseguenza di una sbadata scelta tecnica. E’ bensì il prodotto della consapevole

scelta politica di svuotare la funzione sociale dell’università pubblica come strumento di coesione,

mobilità e produzione di conoscenza. Da un lato, le telematiche continuano a beneficiare di regole

di favore nei requisiti di accreditamento: basti pensare che hanno quintuplicato (+468%) i propri

iscritti nell’ultimo decennio. Dall’altra, gli atenei pubblici vengono spinti verso una gestione sempre

più contabile e di pura sopravvivenza, che azzera la missione culturale delle università e la loro

capacità strategica.

Non sorprende, ma preoccupa, che la Conferenza dei rettori (la Crui) si divida tra chi gioca la

propria partita da una posizione di vantaggio e chi si appiattisce sulla linea della ministra, per

affinità politica o per timore. Rettori forti in casa propria, deboli di fronte al governo (con solo

alcune, pochissime, voci fuori dal coro). Un’amara delusione, perché sarebbe invece possibile

costruire un fronte comune di opposizione a una politica ormai pluriennale di strozzamento

dell’università. Da chi rappresenta la voce delle comunità universitarie, ci si aspetterebbe ben altra

visione.

Il quadro si completa con l’offensiva sulla governance: la riforma del reclutamento, già approvata al

Senato, che abolisce l’ASN e spinge ad un salto nel vuoto, tra rischi di localismo e opacità nella

gestione dei concorsi (difficile, ad oggi, prevederne le conseguenze); la riforma del Cun, che lo

relegherà a una posizione di subalternità rispetto al ministero, con la rappresentanza di ricercatori e

studenti tagliata; la (per ora arenata) riforma proposta della commissione presieduta da Ernesto

Galli della Loggia, che mirerebbe a rafforzare ulteriormente i rettori e i consigli di amministrazione

a scapito della partecipazione delle comunità universitarie.
